title: 'Fast Tech': Cheap Gadgets Cause Costly E-Waste
paragraphs: You have a long train trip, but you forgot your headphones. No drama — you'll just buy a cheap pair at a kiosk in the station.
Your phone is only at 56% charge, too — you'd better buy a cheap charger too. It's also pretty hot, and the kiosk has some cheap electric fans …

Products like these are often called "fast tech." Like fast fashion — clothing made to be worn just a few times and then discarded — gadgets like these are cheap and convenient, but quickly create waste.
A recent survey found that 90% of Europeans own at least one "fast tech" product — and 78% bought one in the past year.
The WEEE Forum, a Belgium-based organization focused on e-waste, surveyed over 10,000 Europeans in July.

Among those who'd bought fast tech, 58% said they could remember a product they'd used for no more than six months. That figure includes 9% of buyers who remember using a product just once, and 3% who remember discarding one without using it!

Often, these products aren't disposed of properly. Just 27% of participants said they remember taking at least one unwanted fast tech item to a recycling center or waste facility, and 19% remember taking one to a collection point in a store.
But 23% have put at least one in with regular household waste, 21% have put one in with plastic recycling, and 7% have put one in a street bin.
Fast tech contains useful resources like metals that could be recycled and reused.

These gadgets also often contain lithium batteries, which can be hazardous. A 2019 WEEE Forum survey found that 36% of European collection, sorting, transportation and recycling facilities for electronic waste had had a severe "thermal incident" in the last four years — including fires, smoke and even explosions — caused by batteries.
The WEEE Forum suggests that before people buy fast tech, they think about whether they really need it, if they could get it second hand, and how they would eventually recycle it.
